strengths: Clear, well-motivated mechanistic story that starts from a simple 1D quadratic counterexample (Fig. 2) showing Adam diverges/spikes where GD does not, cleanly isolating the adaptive preconditioner as the culprit distinct from loss-landscape geometry.

Solid theoretical grounding: derivation of the 'preconditioned Hessian' stability threshold for Adam, proof that the asymmetric preconditioned Hessian is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues (Lem. B.1), a three-term recursion stability condition incorporating momentum (Lem. B.2), and a fully worked five-phase theorem for the 1D quadratic case (Thm. B.1) with a full proof.

The gradient-directional curvature predictor λ_grad is a meaningful refinement over the naive λ_max>2/η criterion, and the paper convincingly shows (Figs. 4,5,6,7) that λ_max alone produces false positives while λ_grad (and its 'sustained' variant for Transformers) aligns closely with actual spike onset.

Reasonably broad empirical validation spanning FNNs, CNNs, and Transformers, including qualitative decomposition of the spike into interpretable phases (vt decay, eigenvalue exceedance, gradient-eigenvector alignment, vt recovery) that is consistent across settings.

Practically useful discussion of mitigation (increasing ε, adjusting β1/β2) with directly demonstrated experiments (Fig. 5f, Fig. D9) showing spikes can be suppressed, and an interesting taxonomy of spike types (neutral/beneficial/malignant/catastrophic) linking spikes to generalization outcomes.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architectures, and dataset descriptions are provided in Appendix E for all experiments.
weaknesses: Most empirical demonstrations are single training runs on a single model/task per architecture (no seeds, no aggregate statistics, no quantitative precision/recall of the λ_grad predictor vs. actual spikes), so the generality and robustness of the claimed mechanism is not statistically established.

Due to the cost of Hessian eigenvalue computation, CNN/Transformer experiments use small data subsets (50 or 1000 CIFAR-10 images) or a fairly small/synthetic Transformer setup, raising concerns about whether the mechanism holds at the realistic scales (e.g., LLM pretraining) that motivate the paper (PaLM spikes are cited in Sec. 2 but never tested).

The 'sustained spike predictor' introduced for the Transformer case (Sec. 5.3) is an ad hoc patch (a 3-step min-window heuristic) without a principled derivation of why or for how long λ_grad must remain elevated, weakening the paper's central claim of a precise, theoretically grounded predictor.

The formal five-phase theorem (Thm. B.1) is proven only for a 1D quadratic with β1=0; the paper's high-dimensional, non-convex claims rest on this simplified case plus qualitative empirical analogy, so the theoretical guarantees don't extend rigorously to the main experimental settings.

The distinction from prior explanations (e.g., Molybog et al. 2023's near-zero gradient/second-moment spike mechanism, Cohen et al. 2023's AEoS) is somewhat incremental; the core empirical observation that vt lags behind gt and decays exponentially has significant conceptual overlap with existing literature, and the paper does not quantitatively disentangle its contribution from the LLAS hypothesis it aims to distinguish itself from, despite claiming this as a key contribution.
Mitigation strategies discussed (increasing ε, reducing β2) are already known from cited prior work (Cattaneo and Shigida, 2025), so the paper's actionable contribution beyond diagnosis is limited.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and previously under-explained phenomenon (Adam loss spikes), with a fairly complete theoretical story spanning derivation, formal proofs (Lemma B.1/B.2, Theorem B.1 for the 1D quadratic case), and multi-architecture empirical validation (FNN, CNN, Transformer).

The derivation of the 'adaptive preconditioned Hessian' stability threshold and the extension from a scalar 2/\eta condition to the gradient-directional curvature predictor \lambda_grad is a clean, testable refinement over the naive \lambda_max(H_hat) > 2/\eta criterion, and the paper shows convincingly in several settings that \lambda_max alone over-predicts spikes while \lambda_grad better localizes them.

Extensive supplementary experiments (Appendices C, D) probing hyperparameter sensitivity (\beta_2, \epsilon), spike categorization (neutral/beneficial/malignant/catastrophic), and simple mitigation strategies (increasing \epsilon or clipping v_t) add practical texture to the mechanistic claims.

The five-phase narrative (decay of preconditioner -> instability onset -> preconditioner recovery -> loss decay) is intuitively coherent and is checked against the empirical eigenvalue/gradient-norm traces across all tested settings.
weaknesses: The central quadratic-approximation machinery is explicitly acknowledged to break down exactly in the regime that matters most (e.g., Fig. 4(a): \lambda_max(H_t) exceeds 2/\eta transiently early in training without a spike because 'the Hessian varies rapidly and the quadratic approximation assumption may not hold'), which undercuts the rigor of the core stability argument in precisely the high-curvature/non-stationary regime under study.

All experiments are conducted at very small scale (CNNs trained on 50-1000 CIFAR-10 images, ~3,000-500,000 parameter models, ~10M-parameter Transformers on synthetic tasks) specifically to make Hessian eigenvalue computation tractable; the paper does not validate the mechanism on realistic large-scale/LLM training where loss spikes are most consequential (the motivating PaLM/OPT examples in the intro and related work are never actually tested), leaving significant doubt about whether the mechanism generalizes to the regimes practitioners care about.

The claimed distinctness from the lower-loss-as-sharper (LLAS) landscape hypothesis is asserted rather than cleanly demonstrated; the conclusion itself admits 'it is possible that both the geometry of the loss landscape and the preconditioners jointly contribute,' and no controlled experiment isolates the preconditioner effect from landscape sharpening effects in the multi-layer, non-toy experiments.

Overlap with prior work is understated: Molybog et al. (2023) already reported that gradient/second-moment estimates decay to near-zero and then spike upon encountering a large gradient — essentially the same decay-then-spike mechanism described here — and Cohen et al. (2023) already formalized Adaptive EoS with a preconditioned Hessian threshold. The paper's incremental contribution over these appears to be primarily the \lambda_grad refinement and phase narrative, but this is not clearly delineated against Molybog's already-similar finding.

The 'sustained spike predictor' introduced in Sec. 5.3 (a 3-step min-window heuristic) appears to be introduced post hoc specifically to patch failure cases where instantaneous \lambda_grad crossings did not correspond to actual spikes in the Transformer experiment; no principled justification or generalizable rule for the window length is given, raising concerns about overfitting the predictor to observed data.

No quantitative evaluation (e.g., precision/recall, false-positive/false-negative rates across many spikes) of the proposed predictors is reported; validation is qualitative/visual on a handful of individually highlighted spikes per figure, which is not fully convincing as rigorous verification of a 'predictor.'

The proposed mitigation strategies (increasing \epsilon or \beta_1, decreasing \beta_2) are already known/suggested in prior literature (e.g., Cattaneo and Shigida 2025), so the paper's actionable contribution beyond mechanistic explanation is limited.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely novel and distinct mechanism for Adam loss spikes (adaptive preconditioner decay decoupling from current gradient information) that is clearly differentiated from the prior lower-loss-as-sharper (LLAS) landscape hypothesis, using a simple but compelling counterexample (constant-curvature quadratic function) where Adam still spikes.

Provides rigorous theoretical backing: a clean stability analysis deriving the 'Adam preconditioned Hessian' Hat{H}_t and its 2/eta threshold, plus a fully worked closed-form five-phase theorem (Thm B.1) for the 1D quadratic case with explicit bounds on phase transition times, giving mechanistic and not just empirical grounding.

Introduces and validates a refined predictor, gradient-directional curvature lambda_grad, showing convincingly (via targeted ablations in Fig. 4 and Fig. 7) that lambda_max(Hat{H}_t) > 2/eta alone is necessary but not sufficient, and that spikes require sustained alignment of the gradient with the unstable eigendirection -- a nontrivial and well-supported refinement over prior EoS-style criteria.

Broad and consistent empirical validation across diverse settings (1D/2D quadratics, FNNs, CNNs on CIFAR-10, and Transformers on sequence learning), with actual Hessian/preconditioned-Hessian eigenvalue tracking via Hessian-vector-product power iteration, second-moment decay-rate fitting, and cosine-similarity/trajectory-projection analyses that corroborate the proposed mechanism from multiple angles.

Practical significance: identifies concrete, tested mitigation levers (increasing epsilon, adjusting beta1/beta2) and connects the phenomenon to a useful taxonomy of spike outcomes (neutral/beneficial/malignant/catastrophic) with train/test loss evidence, adding value beyond pure diagnosis.
Reasonably strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter and dataset descriptions for every figure are given in Appendix E, and proofs are provided in full in Appendix B.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery (quadratic Taylor approximation, the fully rigorous five-phase theorem) is derived only for a scalar/1D quadratic loss; extension to high-dimensional, non-convex neural network losses is empirically motivated but not theoretically proven, and the paper itself notes the quadratic approximation may break down during rapid-loss-change phases, which is precisely when spikes occur -- somewhat undercutting the applicability of the core theory to the phenomena of most interest.

The 'sustained spike predictor' introduced for the Transformer experiment (a hand-picked +-1 iteration smoothing window) appears to be an ad hoc post-hoc fix to make the predictor match observed spikes, without principled justification for why this particular window size is appropriate or how it would generalize to other settings/scales.

Despite claiming the preconditioner mechanism is 'distinct' from the LLAS landscape hypothesis, no direct quantitative comparison (e.g., applying the LLAS predictor to the same experiments and showing it fails where lambda_grad succeeds) is provided; the distinction rests mainly on the introductory toy quadratic example and qualitative arguments, and the conclusion itself admits the two mechanisms may jointly contribute, weakening the strength of the central claim.

Experimental scale is fairly small (CNNs trained on 50-1000 CIFAR-10 images, an 8-layer/10M-parameter Transformer on a synthetic compositional task) due to the computational cost of Hessian eigenvalue estimation; it remains unclear whether the mechanism and predictors generalize to the large-scale LLM pretraining regime where loss spikes are most practically important and originally motivated the LLAS/Adam-instability literature (e.g., PaLM, OPT).

No reporting of variance across random seeds/multiple runs for the key claims (e.g., spike prediction accuracy, decay-rate fits), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported thresholds and fitted decay rates.

The mitigation experiments (increasing epsilon or clipping v_t) are demonstrated only on the small FNN function-approximation setup, not on the CNN or Transformer settings, limiting confidence that the proposed practical fixes scale to more realistic training regimes.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear, well-motivated mechanistic explanation for loss spikes in Adam — the 'decoupling' of the second-moment estimator vt from the instantaneous squared gradient — and distinguishes this cleanly from prior landscape-geometry (LLAS) and EoS-based explanations, with a concrete counterexample (quadratic loss where Adam spikes but GD converges smoothly) that convincingly rules out landscape geometry alone as the cause.

Substantial rigorous theoretical support for the simplified (1D quadratic) setting: closed-form stability conditions for the adaptive and momentum mechanisms (Prop 4.1/4.2), a full five-stage characterization proven as a theorem (Thm 5.1), and a result showing standard learning-rate decay does not eliminate the instability (Thm 5.2), all with complete proofs in the appendix.

The proposed gradient-directional curvature predictor λgrad(Ĥt) is theoretically derived (Thm D.1, exact necessary/sufficient condition) and empirically shown to outperform the naive λmax criterion for anticipating spikes across GD and Adam, in low- and high-dimensional settings.

Very extensive empirical validation spanning FNNs, CNNs (CIFAR-10), ViT, ResNet, and Transformers at multiple scales (10M and 187M parameters, real large-scale pretraining on SlimPajama), plus systematic ablations across alternative adaptive optimizers (Adagrad, RMSProp, Adafactor) and hyperparameter sweeps (β1, β2) that consistently corroborate the proposed mechanism.

Practically useful and actionable finding (reducing β2 mitigates spikes) that is consistent with independent practices already adopted in large-scale LLM training (e.g., LLaMA), lending external validity to the claims.

Transparent limitations, reproducibility, and ethics statements; computational feasibility of the proposed diagnostic (power iteration / single Hessian-vector product) is explicitly discussed and made practical for large models.
Thoughtful additional discussion (spike taxonomy: neutral/benign/malignant/catastrophic) that adds nuance beyond a purely 'spikes are bad' narrative, opening interesting future directions.
weaknesses: The rigorous theoretical results are confined to the 1D quadratic case; extension to high-dimensional, non-convex neural network training rests entirely on empirical correlation rather than formal proof, and the paper's own 'frozen-time'/quasi-static justification for combining β1 and β2 preconditioning effects (Remark 4.4) is heuristic rather than rigorously established for the genuinely time-varying Adam dynamics.

The primary mitigation strategies proposed (reducing β2, increasing ε) are already known/used empirically in practice (as the paper itself notes citing LLaMA etc.); the contribution is more explanatory than a genuinely new remedy, which somewhat limits the practical novelty despite the mechanistic insight.

The spike-type taxonomy (neutral/benign/malignant/catastrophic) is presented with only illustrative examples and no principled criterion for distinguishing categories, leaving this contribution largely descriptive and deferred to future work.

Reliance on Hessian-vector products for λmax and λgrad, while argued to be tractable via power iteration, still adds non-trivial computational and implementation overhead, and the paper acknowledges this becomes prohibitive beyond ~200M parameters, limiting confidence that the mechanism has been validated at truly large (billion-parameter) production LLM scale.

Stochastic minibatch noise substantially complicates precise spike prediction, requiring an ad hoc 'sustained predictor' (min over neighboring steps) whose introduction, while empirically effective, is not theoretically justified and could mask cases where the underlying theory does not cleanly transfer to the stochastic setting.

The manuscript is very dense with a large appendix-heavy structure; some central claims (e.g., the multiplicative composability of temporal and spatial preconditioning) are asserted with intuitive rather than fully formal justification, which could affect confidence in edge cases.

strengths: The paper provides a coherent, well-motivated mechanistic account of loss spikes in Adam, clearly distinguishing itself from the landscape-based LLAS hypothesis with a compelling counterexample (Adam spiking on a quadratic function with tiny learning rates, where GD converges smoothly).

Substantial and rigorous theoretical contribution for the 1D/quadratic setting, including full proofs of a five-stage characterization theorem (Thm 5.1) and a result showing decaying learning-rate schedules cannot avoid the instability for large β2 (Thm 5.2), plus a clean derivation (Thm D.1) of the exact necessary-and-sufficient condition for a loss increase via directional curvature.

The proposed predictor λgrad(Ĥt) is a genuine, testable refinement over the naive λmax criterion, and the paper convincingly demonstrates empirically (GD and Adam, FNN/CNN/Transformer) that λmax exceeding 2/η is necessary but not sufficient, while λgrad tracks spike onset far more precisely.

Very extensive empirical validation spanning toy quadratics, FNNs, CNNs, ViT, ResNet, small (10M) and large-scale (187M, 100B-token) Transformers, and multiple adaptive optimizers (RMSProp, Adagrad, Adafactor) in the appendix, lending good external validity to the core claims.

The practical recommendation (reduce β2) is actionable, cheap to test, and is shown to reduce spike frequency at both small and large scale; the paper notes this aligns with practices already adopted in some large-scale LLM training recipes, strengthening real-world relevance.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (1D theory vs. high-dim empirical generalization, minibatch noise complicating exact prediction, computational cost of Hessian-vector products at scale) and provides an interesting exploratory taxonomy of spike types (neutral/benign/malignant/catastrophic) as a direction for future work.
weaknesses: The rigorous theoretical results are essentially confined to 1D quadratic objectives (and often β1 = 0), which is a considerable simplification; the extension to high-dimensional, non-convex, momentum-driven training relies entirely on empirical corroboration rather than formal analysis, and the paper's own Remark 4.5/4.6 justifications for composing the temporal and spatial preconditioners into a single Ĥt (frozen-time/quasi-static assumptions) are heuristic rather than proven.

The core "decoupling" mechanism—an EMA with large β2 lagging behind instantaneous squared gradients—is a fairly intuitive consequence of exponential moving averages; the paper's novelty claim over Cohen et al. (2023)'s AEoS framework rests mainly on making this lag/threshold relationship more precise, which is a meaningful but somewhat incremental advance rather than a qualitatively new mechanism.

The "sustained spike predictor" (a min over three consecutive λgrad values) introduced to handle minibatch noise is an ad hoc post-hoc fix that is not derived from the theory, which weakens the claimed tightness of the gradient-directional-curvature explanation in realistic stochastic settings.

No head-to-head comparison against other proposed loss-spike mitigation techniques mentioned in the paper (sandwich normalization, σ-Reparam, scale-distribution decoupling); the paper only validates its own remedy (reducing β2 / increasing ε) without benchmarking relative effectiveness or trade-offs (e.g., convergence speed cost) against these alternatives.

The specific empirical constant (η/√v̂t threshold ≈38) reported for the toy 1D example is not clearly shown to be a general/universal quantity versus an artifact of the particular hyperparameter range tested, and its broader significance is unclear.

The four-way spike taxonomy (neutral/benign/malignant/catastrophic) in Appendix E is an interesting but underdeveloped contribution—no predictive criteria are given to anticipate which category a spike will fall into, leaving this as a purely descriptive, exploratory addendum.

The paper is very dense, with most of the rigorous proofs and several key validation figures relegated to a lengthy appendix, making the core theoretical claims difficult to fully verify without extensive cross-referencing, and the main text sometimes over-claims generality (e.g., 'generalizes well') for results that are ultimately empirical pattern-matching rather than formally established for the high-dimensional/non-convex regime.

strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated mechanistic explanation for loss spikes in Adam that goes beyond the prior landscape-geometry (LLAS) hypothesis, using a clean counterexample (quadratic loss, Fig. 2) to show that geometry alone cannot explain the phenomenon.

Strong theoretical foundation: rigorous propositions and theorems (Prop. 4.1/4.2, Theorem 5.1/5.2, Theorem D.1) with complete proofs in the appendix characterizing stability conditions for both the adaptive and momentum mechanisms and formalizing a five-stage life cycle of a spike for the 1D quadratic case.

The proposed gradient-directional curvature predictor λgrad(Ĥt) is a genuinely useful and non-trivial refinement over the naive λmax criterion, and is convincingly shown (via GD and Adam comparisons, Fig. 4) to more precisely anticipate spike onset, including with a practical 'sustained predictor' variant for noisy mini-batch settings.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of scales and architectures — FNN, CNN, ViT, ResNet, small Transformers (10M), and a 187M LLaMA-style model trained on 100B tokens — lending credibility that the mechanism is not an artifact of toy settings.

Practical, actionable recommendation (reducing β2) is both theoretically motivated and empirically validated, and is consistent with existing practice in large-scale LLM training (e.g., Llama, PanGu), strengthening real-world relevance.

Thorough appendix with numerous ablations (different optimizers: Adagrad, RMSProp, Adafactor; different β1/β2; delay mechanisms in GD; ε and vt-clipping interventions) that substantially strengthen the robustness of the claimed mechanism.

Honest and clearly delineated limitations section, correctly scoping the rigorous theory to the 1D quadratic setting and acknowledging computational constraints and open questions (e.g., spike-type classification, disentangling landscape vs. preconditioner effects).
weaknesses: The fully rigorous theoretical analysis (five-stage theorem, decaying LR theorem) is confined to the 1D scalar quadratic case; extension to high-dimensional, non-convex neural network settings is only empirically supported, and the 'dual preconditioning' factorization (Eq. 7) combining momentum and adaptive effects relies on a frozen-time/LTI heuristic (Remark 4.4) rather than a rigorous LTV analysis.

The intuitive explanation for why decoupling occurs (Remark 4.7, based on 'small parameter updates') is somewhat informal and could benefit from a more rigorous derivation, especially given that this decoupling is the paper's central causal claim.

In stochastic mini-batch training, exact spike timing prediction is compromised by noise, and the paper's fix (a 'sustained' min-over-window predictor) is a practical heuristic rather than a principled solution, reducing the rigor of the real-world validation somewhat.

The relationship to Cohen et al. (2023)'s AEoS framework is close (the preconditioned Hessian and 2/η threshold are essentially the same construct); while the authors argue their decoupling mechanism and λgrad predictor are novel refinements, the incremental nature of this contribution relative to AEoS could be more sharply delineated.

Scalability of the Hessian-vector-product-based eigenvalue tracking beyond ~200M parameters remains a practical bottleneck, limiting how far the empirical validation of the theory can be pushed toward truly large-scale models where spikes are most consequential.

The four-way taxonomy of spike types (neutral/benign/malignant/catastrophic) in Appendix E is an interesting but underdeveloped side contribution; no rigorous or automatable criterion is given to distinguish these cases, leaving practical actionability of this analysis limited.

The dense mathematical presentation and large number of figures/experiments, while thorough, make the paper's core narrative arc harder to follow in places, and would benefit from tighter integration of the extensive appendix material into a more streamlined main narrative.
